podcast.title: Early Lineup with Saxophone
podcast.body: The 1986 4-track cassette lineup of On a Friday included a saxophone player, and Jonny Greenwood had not yet joined the band. "At the time, Anna Friday had a saxophone player and did not yet include Colin Greenwood's younger brother Johnny."

podcast.title: Name Origin
podcast.body: The band adopted the name "On a Friday" because their rehearsal time was limited to Friday afternoons in the music room of Oxford Shears Abingdon School due to their studies. "Studies got in the way of rehearsal time except on Friday afternoons in the school's music room, which is how the band came to be known as Anna Friday."

xref.title: Hiatus for College (1991)
xref.body: In 1991, "On a Friday" entered an extended hiatus as all five members pursued higher education at different universities. Ed O'Brien went to Manchester University, Colin Greenwood studied English literature at Cambridge, Phil Selway also studied English literature at Liverpool University, and Johnny Greenwood enrolled in both music and psychology programs at Oxford. Tom York decided to take a year off before attending university. "In 1997, a 1991 on a Friday went on an extended sort of hiatus."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Manic Hedgehog Tape (1991)
xref.body: This was a five-song cassette that "On a Friday" sold for three pounds at the local indie record store, Manic Hedgehog, where Colin Greenwood worked. Colin strategically "slipped a copy of this cassette" to any record label representatives who visited the store. This grassroots promotion led to an unprecedented 25 record company reps attending their pivotal gig at the Jericho Tavern. "That cassette ended up being referred to as appropriately the Manic Hedgehog tape and it featured songs like this. It's called Philip a Chicken."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Name Change to Radiohead (1991)
xref.body: After signing with EMI, the label expressed dissatisfaction with the name "On a Friday" and instructed the band to find a new one. Various suggestions were considered, including "Jude the Obscure" (deemed "too obscure" from the Thomas Hardy novel), "Music" (liked by Tom but rejected), and "Gravitates" (which "didn't have the right ring to it"). The definitive name, "Radiohead," was discovered when someone retrieved a 1986 Talking Heads album, "True Stories," from Tom York's DJ collection, which featured a song of the same name. The name change officially occurred at the end of 1991. "And so it came to pass that at the end of 1991, on a Friday, became known as Radiohead."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Record Deal with EMI (1991)
xref.body: By the end of 1991, "On a Friday" was actively pursued by various record companies, culminating in a six-album deal with EMI, signed on December 21, 1991. This deal marked a significant milestone, although it came with a stipulation for the band to change its name. "On December 21, 1991, they signed an album deal with EMI."

xref.title: "On a Friday" Name Origin
xref.body: The band originally adopted the name "On a Friday" because Friday was the sole day of the week when all the members could gather for rehearsals. "As it turns out, the only day the guys could rehearse was Friday. So the band became known as on a Friday."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: College and Jobs
xref.body: Colin secured a coveted spot at Cambridge University, where he pursued studies in English literature. During his pre-Radiohead years, he worked at two local record stores: Manic Hedgehog and Our Price. At these stores, he proactively distributed "On a Friday" demos to visiting record company representatives. He also held a position as the school's entertainment director. "Colin landed a hard-to-get-spotted Cambridge where he studied English literature."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Continued Rehearsals (Early 1990s)
xref.body: Despite their individual college pursuits, the members of "On a Friday" maintained their musical connection by meeting once a month to rehearse on Fridays. During this period, they occasionally recorded their material on a cheap tape recorder, amassing approximately 15 original songs by the close of 1990. "Meanwhile, once a month, all the on-off Friday guys would still get together and rehearse on Friday, of course, and applaud what they might do together once this school thing was out of the way."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early "On a Friday" Member
xref.body: Razz Peterson was a saxophonist and a member of "On a Friday" during the recording of their 1986 five-track cassette. He was part of the band's lineup before Johnny Greenwood joined. "Johnny Greenwood is not part of the band yet, but a sax player named Razz Peterson is."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Lineup and Instrumentation
xref.body: In its formative years as "On a Friday," the band's instrumentation was quite fluid and experimental. Johnny Greenwood, who joined around age 13, often played harmonica, recorder, and occasionally keyboards. At different points, the group featured "an all-female horn section" and even three saxophone players, despite acknowledging that the sax players "weren't very good, but at least they were having a good time." "Now at first, on a Friday was all over the place. Johnny played harmonica, sometimes the recorder, complete keyboards, every once in a while."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Early Music Involvement
xref.body: Johnny began his musical journey in his early teens with his brother Colin, influenced by their older sister's interest in bands like George Evasion in the Fall. Initially, he attended "On a Friday" practices primarily because Colin was "babysitting him." However, after continuously expressing his desire to participate, he was eventually integrated into the band at approximately age 13, while the other members were 16 or 17. "after hearing him whine about wanting to do something, everybody just gave in and made him part of the band."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: First Proper Demo (Early 1990s)
xref.body: Around the time all five members moved into a semi-detached house near the center of Oxford, "On a Friday" recorded their first professional demo. This three-song cassette cost 300 pounds to produce and was released without a specific title or catalog number. "They recorded their first proper demo. Three songs, 300 pounds."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Joining "On a Friday"
xref.body: Phil Selway was recruited into "On a Friday" from another Abingdon-based group called Jungle Telegraph. His role was to replace the band's "horrible drum machine," Dr. Rhythm. "Phil Selway was drafted in from an Albington group called Jungle Telegraph to replace that horrible drum machine."

xref.title: Oxford Music Scene
xref.body: The Jericho Tavern in Oxford, where "On a Friday" played a crucial gig in October 1991, was "semi-famous at the time for hosting other big-ish Oxford bands" like Supergrass. "the Jericho Tavern, which by the way was semi-famous at the time for hosting other big-ish Oxford bands like Super Grass and Ride and Slow Dive."

xref.body: Slowdive was among the "big-ish Oxford bands" that had achieved semi-fame by playing at the Jericho Tavern, the venue where "On a Friday" had a significant gig in October 1991.
